procedural_history.impugned_order: Judgment of the Madras High Court dated 09.03.2010 in Criminal Appeal No. 1 of 2010, which dismissed the appeal against the Trial Court's decision.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: The Appellant challenged the decision of the Trial Court before the Madras High Court in Criminal Appeal No. 1 of 2010. The High Court dismissed the appeal, upholding the judgment of the Trial Court.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The Appellant approached the Supreme Court by way of a special leave petition challenging the High Court's judgment. The Supreme Court dismissed the appeal, affirming the concurrent findings of fact by the Trial Court and the High Court.

issue.issue_text: Whether the Supreme Court, in an appeal by special leave, should interfere with the concurrent findings of fact on guilt recorded by the Trial Court and the High Court.

facts: The Trial Court and the High Court both found the appellant guilty based on their appreciation of the evidence.
The appellant challenged these concurrent findings of guilt in the Supreme Court through an appeal by special leave.
The challenge was primarily based on what the court described as 'minor discrepancies' in the evidence presented by prosecution witnesses.
law: The Supreme Court has a general practice of not interfering with concurrent findings of fact recorded by lower courts in an appeal by special leave.
An appeal by special leave is not treated as a regular appeal or another forum for the reappreciation of evidence.
The Court will only interfere in rare and exceptional cases to prevent a grave or serious miscarriage of justice.

Interference is justified only if it is established that: (1) the finding is based on no evidence; (2) the finding is perverse (one that no reasonable person could reach); (3) the finding is based on inadmissible evidence that is critical to the case; or (4) a vital piece of evidence favouring the convict has been overlooked or disregarded.
application: The Court applied its established legal principles to the case.
It determined that the appellant's arguments, which focused on minor discrepancies, did not meet the high threshold required for interference.
The Court found that the present case did not fall into any of the exceptional categories, such as being based on no evidence, perversity, or manifest illegality.

Therefore, the Court concluded that it was not appropriate or permissible to re-evaluate or reappraise the evidence that both the Trial Court and the High Court had already found to be worthy of acceptance.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court decided not to interfere with the concurrent findings of guilt. It held that the appellant had not established any of the rare and exceptional grounds, such as perversity or a grave miscarriage of justice, that would warrant reopening the factual findings of the lower courts.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the Supreme Court, in an appeal by special leave, should interfere with the concurrent findings of fact on guilt recorded by the Trial Court and the High Court.
appellant_arguments: The concurrent findings should be overturned due to several shortcomings, lacunae, inconsistencies, and contradictions in the prosecution's case and witness testimonies.
The factors relied upon by the lower courts do not form a complete chain of circumstances that leads to a finding of guilt.
The Trial Court failed to properly put material evidence to the accused to provide an opportunity for explanation.
The appellant relied on an alibi.
respondent_arguments: The prosecution has discharged its burden of proving the appellant's guilt beyond a reasonable doubt.
The benefit of the doubt cannot be stretched to cover minor discrepancies.
The established chain of circumstances leads to no other plausible hypothesis than the guilt of the appellant.
No case for interference in the concurrent findings of the Trial Court and the High Court has been made out.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: The Supreme Court will not re-appreciate evidence or interfere with concurrent findings of fact from the trial court and High Court, except in rare cases where there is a manifest illegality or a grave miscarriage of justice, such as when the finding is perverse, based on no evidence, based on inadmissible evidence, or has overlooked vital evidence.
obiter: A criminal case is proven only through certain and explicit evidence; no person can be convicted on pure moral conviction.
In a case based on circumstantial evidence, the circumstances must be of a conclusive nature and tendency.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: In an appeal by special leave, the Supreme Court will not interfere with concurrent findings of fact on guilt recorded by the Trial Court and the High Court, as it is not the Court's practice to re-appreciate evidence. The Court's overriding and exceptional power is exercised sparingly and only in rare and exceptional cases to prevent a grave or serious miscarriage of justice, such as when findings are perverse, based on no evidence, built on inadmissible evidence, or when vital evidence has been ignored. The present case does not fall into this category.
legal_tests_applied: A concurrent finding of fact cannot be reopened in an appeal by special leave unless it is established: (1) that the finding is based on no evidence or (2) that the finding is perverse, it being such as no reasonable person could have arrived at even if the evidence was taken at its face value or (3) the finding is based and built on inadmissible evidence, which evidence, if excluded from vision, would negate the prosecution case or substantially discredit or impair it or (4) some vital piece of evidence which would tilt the balance in favour of the convict has been overlooked, disregarded, or wrongly discarded.

The overriding and exceptional power under Article 136 is to be exercised sparingly and only in furtherance of the cause of justice, particularly when the judgment under appeal has resulted in grave miscarriage of justice by some misapprehension or misreading of evidence or by ignoring material evidence.

An appeal by special leave where the trial court and the High Court have concurrently returned findings of fact cannot be dealt with as if it were another forum for reappreciation of evidence, unless the assessment is vitiated by an error of law or procedure, misreading of evidence, or disregard for judicial norms leading to serious prejudice or injustice.
why_appellant_lost: The appellant failed to demonstrate that the case met the high threshold for interference, as the challenge to the conviction was based mainly on minor discrepancies in the evidence, which are not sufficient grounds for the Court to reappraise the evidence.

The Court determined that the present case was not one where the concurrent findings were based on no evidence, were perverse, were based on inadmissible evidence, or where vital evidence was overlooked.
The Court affirmed that a wholesome reappreciation of evidence is not within the scope of an appeal by special leave against concurrent findings of fact.
why_respondent_won: The respondent successfully argued that no case for interference with the concurrent findings of fact was made out, a position the Court ultimately adopted.
The Court's established practice is not to re-appreciate evidence in such appeals, and the respondent's position aligned with this judicial principle.
The Court accepted the principle that reasonable doubt must not be a 'trivial' or 'merely possible' doubt, and that minor discrepancies would not adversely affect the prosecution's case.
policy_considerations: The Court's power under Article 136 is an 'overriding and exceptional power' that is 'to be exercised sparingly and only in furtherance of cause of justice' to prevent 'grave or serious miscarriage of justice'.

An appeal by special leave against concurrent findings is not a matter of regular appeal, and the Court will not enter into a reappreciation of evidence so as to take a different view than the lower courts, except in rare and exceptional cases of manifest illegality.
